name: AI in Health Care Delivery
blurb: How hospitals, practices and payers use AI in patient care and its administration.
title: AI in Health Care Delivery
answer: AI in care delivery is spreading but unevenly. About a third of US hospitals reported using AI in a 2025 national study, ambient AI scribes are the fastest growing tool, and the main constraints are privacy rules, evidence that tools help patients, and the work of fitting them into clinical routines.

reading.body:
About a third of US hospitals were using AI in 2025, and another quarter planned to start within a year. That is real adoption, but it leaves most hospitals on the outside, and it says nothing about how deeply the tools are used where they exist.

The pattern is that AI enters care delivery through administration and documentation before clinical judgment. Ambient scribes are the fastest growing tool because they sit beside the visit rather than inside the decision, and the constraints named are privacy rules, evidence of patient benefit, and the work of fitting tools into clinical routines. Those are not compute constraints. They are legal, evidentiary, and organisational ones, which is why adoption is uneven across institutions rather than uniform across the country.

The regulatory line matters for what comes next. The FDA's 2022 guidance on clinical decision support software sets which tools are regulated as devices, so the same capability can be a documentation aid or a regulated product depending on how it is framed. The cited literature runs from 2009 to 2023, and the most cited paper is from 2019, so the research base predates the current generation of language models.

What the data does not cover is cost, staffing, or outcomes. It names one vendor, OpenAI, and one deployment list, and it does not say whether any of these tools improved patient care.

The adoption number and the constraint list describe the same thing from two directions. A third of hospitals use AI and a quarter plan to, which means the decision to adopt is not gated on capability, since the capability is available to all of them at once. It is gated on the three named constraints, and each of those is local: a privacy review is local, a fit into clinical routine is local, and evidence of patient benefit has to be assembled institution by institution. That is why the distribution is uneven rather than a wave.

The tool that grows fastest is the one that touches the least. An ambient scribe sits beside the visit and drafts the note, so it never enters the decision, which keeps it on the documentation side of the FDA's 2022 line rather than the device side. The same underlying model, pointed at diagnosis instead of dictation, would cross that line. The regulatory boundary, not the technical one, decides which products exist.

The research base is older than the products. The cited papers run from 2009 to 2023 and the most cited is from 2019, before the current generation of language models. So the evidence constraint named in the adoption data is not a gap that existing literature can close. The studies that would answer whether these tools help patients largely have not been run yet.

How many US hospitals actually use AI?
31.5 percent were current users in a 2025 national study published in JAMA Network Open, and 24.7 percent planned to adopt within a year.

Why are ambient AI scribes growing faster than other clinical AI?
They sit beside the visit rather than inside the clinical decision, which keeps clinical risk low and keeps them on the documentation side of the FDA's 2022 clinical decision support guidance.

What is actually stopping hospitals from adopting more AI?
The data names three constraints: privacy rules, evidence that tools help patients, and the work of fitting them into clinical routines. It does not rank them or measure their relative weight.

Does the FDA regulate clinical AI as a medical device?
The FDA issued final guidance on clinical decision support software in 2022 setting which tools are regulated as devices. The data states the guidance exists and what it governs, but not which specific products fall on which side.

Which companies are deploying AI in hospitals?
The data names OpenAI, through OpenAI for Healthcare, with deployments at Boston Children's Hospital, Cedars-Sinai, HCA Healthcare and UCSF. It names no other vendor.

Do these tools improve patient care?
The data does not say. It names evidence of patient benefit as a constraint on adoption but reports no outcome, cost, or staffing result for any deployed tool.
